utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. May I raise just one very brief housekeeping matter before we commence, that is the following: In keeping with our customary practice, Mr. Robinson and I agreed upon the limited portions of previous statements that were raised by the -- during the cross-examination of witness Dodik, and we've provided to the Registrar a list of those specific references contained in 65 ter 24921 and 24924. So -- and we would ask that those be admitted with the -- as I say, with the agreement and exchange of information with the Defence and based on our customary practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. So they are uploaded onto e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a brief look and come back to this issue. Mr. Galic and Mr. Piletta-Zanin, with respect to the issues raised by Mr. Galic yesterday, the Chamber is still looking into the matter, particularly Chamber inquired of the Detention Unit as to whether there could be a way in which an observation could be performed without necessarily awakening the detainee, and the Chamber was told by the Detention Unit that the commander will -- commander would consult the medical doctor as to the appropriate interval. We'll come back to this issue very soon. Having said that, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies, good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, even though we are in a hurry and I wish us to finish as soon as possible, I would ask you to make pauses and speak slowly. We are still dealing with your relations with the UNPROFOR so if we could please have 1D06320. Yes, this is your report dated the 19th of January, regular combat report. 1993 is the year. In the first paragraph, about the enemy you say that the enemy fired from all kinds of weapons, especially the sniper fire and wounded a member of UNPROFOR on the Paolina-Hotin [phoen] road. And under 4, unusual incidents, wounding of an UNPROFOR member, commendation to our soldiers from the Vogosca Brigade who managed to pull out the UNPROFOR member who would certainly have died. Can you tell us what that was about.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a lot is already explained in the -- in item 1. And here, in item 4, in a way, the development is described. So there was fire. I think that it was even necessary to pull out one UNPROFOR member, as far as I remember. I'm not sure if this was the situation. In any case, they assisted the UNPROFOR members, and that was why they were commended. And obviously the forces of the BH Army 1st Corps fired at UNPROFOR. So that would be the answer to your question, in brief. Perhaps I still owe you a part of my answer from yesterday when I talked about relations with UNPROFOR when I said that they did not receive the right information, so I was too short and you -- I was interrupted, so if you would allow me to add something now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as briefly as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have many comments to say, and I wish that I would be given the opportunity to state that before this Tribunal. I started yesterday with sniping incidents and then I continued. But I also wanted to talk the main subjects which are important in order to understand the relations between the UNPROFOR and the Army of Republika Srpska and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and also my own attitude to UNPROFOR. They did not have sufficient information because if General MacKenzie had had sufficient information, he wouldn't have led the JNA column to the Vrojacka [phoen] Street where they then perished. For sure. That's why I think that they did not have sufficient information. I couldn't say because I would accuse General MacKenzie here if I said that he had sufficient information but still he led the column into the ambush laid by the BH Army. And another example involving the same general, MacKenzie, when there were talks, these were events preceding my arrival but they had an impact on the situation as it developed after my arrival. When the talks about the airport were conducted, General MacKenzie was in charge of negotiating with the Serbian side and he promised that there would be a road next to the airport that would link Ilidza to Lukavica. However, that was never realised and so the section the north western part of the front remained cut off. The operational reasons and problems which the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps faced as a result is something that I wouldn't discuss now. But later on I received information during my trial, General Nambiar said the following. It is true that General MacKenzie had promised the road to the Serbs that would link Lukavica with Ilidza, but he was entitled. He did not have the right to do that. So that was some sort of justification for that. However, I do not believe that MacKenzie wanted to deceive the Serbian side. Another issue that is very important. When we were withdrawing from Bjelasnica and Igman on the 14th of August, 1994, and when UNPROFOR was supposed to take over control of the area, when the agreement was made, they believed that they would really hold those areas. But later on we saw that he couldn't take control of the areas but that it was rather the BH Army which entered there and then committed various crimes from there against the army of Republika Srpska, that is to say the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and civilians as well. I couldn't say that they did that deliberately to cause problems for us. Another thing connected to the airport, if I go back to the time when I was in command, the problem with the airport was that freight traffic was allowed in order to supply humanitarian aid and materiel and technical equipment that the UNPROFOR needed. But then they abused it and there were manoeuvres of the BH Army from Sarajevo towards Igman and backwards, and we know that the tunnel below the airport was also dug at the time. When I regularly asked them throughout 1993 and up until the time when the tunnel began to be operational whether someone was digging the tunneling, they would tell me that the tunnel was not being dug. It is interesting. I don't know if they didn't know, but according to some information that we heard, I don't know if the information was correct, but even the UNPROFOR forces were helping with the digging of the tunnel. It's possible that they did. There was a Military Observer here who testified and who said that to this day he doesn't know that a tunnel had been dug even though there is a museum devoted to the digging of the tunnel in Sarajevo. I don't know, I haven't visited it because I have been in detention all the time but I read that in the paper. Another problem that arose and something that we couldn't accept in any way. You must remember it quite well but let me remind you anyway. It was this. When at some point in spring 1994 General van Baal through Cekrcici or rather from Visoko through Cekrcici centre, these six APCs to block off some pieces of equipment which, judging by the US maps, was within the 20-kilometre zone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I got carried away a little bit. Thank you. That those weapons were within the 20 kilometre zone; that is to say, the exclusion zone. Judging by our map, when measured from the centre of the city, they were outside of the 20-kilometre zone which is something I explained to you earlier. And so on. Before this, we made a phone call and we got in touch with the general. General Rose went to London to be knighted at the time and van Baal as his deputy remained there. He did not communicate with us and our command sufficiently so that we would establish precisely where the weapons were, whether it was within the 20 kilometre zone. Later on the Canadian Battalion with 36 APCs, that was a big provocation, a big and serious provocation because they tied up my soldiers in Cekrcici. That was how they entered. Why did they have to tie them up? They could have -- yes, thank you. Did they tie them up because we were friendly to them? When the UNPROFORs came along with their equipment, my soldiers went out to greet them and they arrested them or tied them up. And in that way, they passed by them. Later movements of those forces were blocked and a serious incident could have happened. We discussed that together in Pale. You, Mr. President, General van Baal and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that this is sufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, I leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one observation. The General referred to General Nambiar's testimony in the Galic trial and General Nambiar never testified in the Galic trial. He must have meant somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? Mr. President, would you allow me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it to Mr. Karadzic. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us. Tell us who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant General Nambiar precisely. No one else to mean. Because he was the commander of the UNPROFOR forces in all of Yugoslavia, I think, or something like that. At such a high level. And I said that because his statement was used in my trial. If I need to explain that in more detail, so I'm sure it can be found among the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1D07727.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please have a look at this. The date is the 2nd of April, 1993. And an order is issued on your behalf: Shooting aircraft, taking off or landing from the airport are prohibited most strictly. And then under 2, strictly prohibiting fire against UN forces positioned at the airport. And then it says under 5 that the order also concerns the aircraft carrying humanitarian aid over the SRK zone. Can you tell us how often you issued such orders and why.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have seen in one report that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces were mentioned as possible attackers of an aircraft which was landing, even though later on it was established that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces had not been responsible. In such situations, when things were critical, to put it that way, then I would issue such orders. I suppose that this order was linked with another order about the so-called parachute operation. I'm not sure whether it was the same period, but let me explain what that was about. Namely, we talked with the general who was representative of the US army. I think his name was Johnson. I believe that was his name, but it could have been different. That was how I understood him at the time and how I remember his name. They then wanted to be -- to supply the Muslim forces or men with humanitarian aid by goods that would be thrown with parachutes from aircraft in Igman and in the area towards Gorazde and Srebrenica. But to have those freight aircraft fly there then, they are slow and they are sensitive to any sort of fire, so I issued an order that this part of the agreement had to be observed as well, meaning the flying over of aircraft carrying humanitarian aid. It was interesting that we had made many efforts but not a single package fell on the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or even the Army of Republika Srpska. No aircraft carrying such sort of aid was targeted from the area held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But we had a piece of information about the aircraft that were supplying Igman and the area in the direction of Konjic. I'm not sure where they were throwing the supplies, but it was fired by the BH Army troops. I'm not sure which forces those were. It could have been somebody else not just the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have in e-court 1D01568.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please focus on this. The date is the 24th of July, 1993, for General Milosevic, your deputy, and the Chief of Staff, signed by somebody else for him. We see it's mentioned what the enemy is doing, where he is firing from, Stupsko Brdo, provocations from snipers and infantry weapons and also mortar shells. Two were fired at Grbavica. Sniper firing, one civilian killed by the Zeljeznica stadium. This is what I'm interested in. Item 2, last sentence: "All subordinated units have been strictly warned to prevent incidents between VRS members and UNPROFOR members." So this is a repetition of the warning and a strict warning at that. Can you tell us what made you to repeat these warnings often to try and maintain good relations and prevent and avoid any incidents?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was the situation that existed, and we were also implementing the Lukavac 93 operation. In that situation, UNPROFOR wanted a complete picture of the activities of the front line. They wanted more information so they could monitor what was going on. There was a permanent representative at our forward command post. It was a military observer who observed the operation, and that's probably why this warning was required. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more about this topic. 1D06328, please. 1D06328.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document. It's a cable. We see that it reads: "Prohibition of Conducting Combat Operations Against UNPROFOR and Other International Organisations." In the preamble you say that the Geneva talks are under way and any conflict with UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations would be used for a renewed demonisation of the Serbs and could serve as a motive for making moves detrimental to your people. And under item 2 of the order you say that full protection must be secured for all the UNPROFOR convoys, military observers, and convoys of international organisations who got approval to pass the territory controlled by the VRS. What was the interest of the VRS to provide safety and protection to these international factors and to prohibit fire at them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we remind ourselves of the previous conversation, we will see that the Muslim forces sometimes used the command posts on the positions of the international organisations as places from which they fired at our units. In order to avoid any such activity, this first part of the order is about these things. Neither the equipment nor the command posts or positions of the UN were ever targeted by us. The passage of convoys that had a permit, and if I remember what the situation was like at winter time, because all roads of the SRK were blocked from Tarcin and Hadzici to Sarajevo and other directions too. But if you stop such a convoy, nobody else can pass because there was much snow in the area. But there were probably requests made at check-point or something. I remember an instance when you called and said that a convoy must be let through. There were some problems. The situation wasn't ideal. Certainly not. I said what it was like around Hadzici and Blazuj. And even though the convoys only provided supplies to the part of Sarajevo controlled by the BH Army 1st Corps, they regularly -- they were regularly able to pass. And if I may add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only convoy from Serbia to Sarajevo was led by Fil -- Filaret [phoen], an ecclesiastical dignitary. There were various organisations sending humanitarian aid to their people in Sarajevo, including Muslims and Croats. When they moved closer to Dobrinja and the area controlled by the Muslims, they were stopped and fire was opened at them. Three drivers were injured at the time. I learned of it and it all went through UNPROFOR, and then the convoy entered Sarajevo. That's the only such convoy sent by Serbs from Serbia that made it to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 12, the transcript didn't record that I probably got information from international organisations when I called you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my assumption. Because they were known to contact you and asked for assistance in some situations. But I must mention one more problem. When you issue an order, and I have an order from the Main Staff, then I must report to the Main Staff what I'm supposed to do. Because that's how it has to be in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was page 11, line 20.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, a minute ago you mentioned that our people perceived us as not being treated equally with regard to humanitarian aid. Were there any other reasons, justified or unjustified, to provoke anger in both our soldiers and civilians against international organisations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One thing that made me angry, and the soldiers and the people too, was the fact that we found weapons and ammunition in those convoys. It was also broadcast in the media. I don't know if that content made it to the international media. But we knew that in Sarajevo there were 350.000 people who needed food, so whenever we stopped a convoy, somebody would be hungry. It was hard to say what should be done when weapons have been discovered, and yet the convoy carried valuable supplies. There were units escorting the convoys; mostly Ukrainian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you inform them, did you submit protests to UNPROFOR with regard to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning all these events that were not normal and which we considered as detrimental to our relations and the agreements, the SRK had to implement about a dozen various agreements. Only about cease-fire. Then there were agreements about humanitarian aid. And we wanted to honour all these agreements. There was also the humanitarian commission, the Krajisnik Muratovic commission. Many considered it unimportant, but I thought it was important. I will probably be able to say more about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the other side didn't honour agreement, did you protest to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was not in accordance with the agreements or the safety of the units of the SRK, I sent warnings or information to UNPROFOR or protested pointing out the problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01865, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we wait, let me say that we always strove to take care of things through the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there were also protests from the corps command level.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. We saw that yesterday that there were protests from my level, because we had all these commanders coming to us and our relations were more immediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this protest to UNPROFOR. It's about the behaviour of the enemy during a cease-fire. They are regrouping their forces, seizing territories, inflicting casualties on the civilian population. And toward the end of the first paragraph, it says: "In case they don't stop these actions, the corps will be forced to respond adequately ... it would put in question all efforts," and so on. And the last question: "We ask you to intervene with the [sic] opposing party to stop its actions." Very briefly and if possible just answer yes or no: When the other side violates an agreement, do you have -- do you have a carte blanche to respond immediately?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this situation, we don't have carte blanche. We cannot respond to enemy activity immediately. Wherever possible, we warned of such actions, and wherever UNPROFOR was able to do so, they were supposed to stop the enemy attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 1D06321.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, in this document dated 8 April 1993, we won't go into these shells and the violations of the cease-fire agreement. Instead, I direct your attention to item 9. You inform the Main Staff that this -- the misses, the -- or the shots that missed the runway threatens planes, and so on. Was this a frequent occurrence or what could be done?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this didn't happen often. However, it was rather frequent at the time, and we were -- we didn't understand what was happening, whether -- did they have bad pilots who didn't know how to land or ... But they were all cruising above the SRK. Now it's open to discussion whether that was or was not air-space in which they were allowed to cruise. I am convinced that they did so to observe our territory and take photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06322, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your command is informing the Main Staff on the 24th of April, 1993, about activities. And toward the end of the first paragraph, they say: "They chose the most favourable moment when a lot of people were in the streets." And in item 5 you speak about an extraordinary event: "An UNPROFOR convoy that had set off from Kiseljak towards Sarajevo but was stopped at Kobiljaca because they didn't allow any inspection. And another convoy ... that had set off for Sarajevo was also stopped there because it hadn't been announced and it didn't allow inspection either. Then it goes on to say that: "Four civilians and one soldier were wounded." And the conclusion is: "UNPROFOR forces are attempting to provoke a conflict with our forces since they don't respect their peace mission and the agreements signed." Can we see the next page in both languages. "Forecast: "It is expected that such provocations will continue." In such cases, serious cases, who protests, you or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such more serious situations, once the front line is reached, because that's where Kobiljaca is, and you see that they don't allow inspection of these convoys, this was April 1993 which was a tumultuous month with lots of combat activity, of course, that will give rise to suspicion. I don't know what kind of inspection is mentioned here but at any rate there shouldn't have been any problems. However, if they refuse to be inspected then that is a problem. In such a situation the Main Staff is informed who had a representative, Mr. Indjic, who was in charge of co-operation with UNPROFOR, and he was also a liaison officer between the SRK and the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3469, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at 1D01535? This was issued on the 21st of May, 1995. Under 1, you can see that a tank T-55 was observed in the Sokolje sector. There's a reference to fire against Nedzarici from Stupsko Brdo and Mojmilo. However, under 2 it says: "Our units are observing the cease-fire. UNPROFOR receives our regular protests." What was your experience? Did UNPROFOR have a say with the other side when we -- when it came to cease-fire violations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we see what sort of movements there were -- taking place in the Sokolje sector, we can see that a tank appeared there quite often, so this was nothing new. Our protests were lodged in order to stop the fire that was opened by the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. That is why we sent warnings and protest notes to the UNPROFOR Command, most commonly to the Sarajevo Sector of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is Sokolje; can you tell us? Is it on the outer ring of Sarajevo or is it down-town?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolje is a settlement near Rajlovac. It's a new settlement and its inhabitants are mostly people who had arrived from Sandzak. At least that's what I have been told. I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just for the transcript, it should read not 17593 but 17595. Thank you. When I said 175, it's page 17, line 15, and the year is 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3470, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D01547. Thank you. The date is 10 June 1993. I'm interested in page 3, which is the most important page in this document with regard to the topic that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the conclusion. It says here that artillery and mortar fire has been stepped up. The number of projectiles is growing by the day. And then in the middle it says that the enemy - and the word used here is "poturice" - is supplied with ammunition by UNPROFOR. There's no logical explanation as to the number of shells fired. Did they have a -- an ammunition production --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do -- can we find the passage in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's bullet point 8(b). 8(b). The following page. "Predictions: [In English] We belive that the Turks in Sarajevo are being supplied." [Interpretation] That's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Supplied with ammunition by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of shell production in Sarajevo? If there was, was that production enough to explain such high expenditures?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that we had at the time, they could produce shells, rifle grenades, mortar shells. Those that they produced were obviously different from the originals, but their effect was the same. So they did have some production. However, whenever a convoy arrived in Sarajevo - I don't know why - but I claim here those activities were stepped up and it seemed that they have limitless quantities of ammunition at those times. I don't know why. Was it due to the fact that another order was in place, that they were in a different mood, or they had been supplied with ammunition in a different way? I was not in a position to be the judge of that, but one of the explanations is that they received ammunition from UNPROFOR either by means of those convoys that transported humanitarian aid or in some other way I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was interpreted in the document as Turks, but what does a "poturice" mean, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not a term that I would use. My Chief of Staff used that term until the arrival of Milosevic. He used the term "poturice," but it was a derogatory term for Muslims. When you say "poturice" that means that you're referring to a person who started life as a member of another ethnicity and then became Turk. That would be the interpretation. If I did not make myself clear enough, I can go on explaining because there is more to the term than just this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient. Thank you, Mr. Galic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would have been the ethnicity of those people who then became Turks and adopted Muslim religion?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, the history of the Balkan peninsula, as you know, is very complex, but you can be a member of any ethnic group in order to become a Turk. But in this particular case, those Turks were supposed to have started their life as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like us to see whether that term "poturice" referred to the people as a whole or just to the combatants. Was there any difference there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The general has just said that that is not a word that he uses. It was a word used by his Chief of Staff. So how can he now speculate on what his Chief of Staff might have meant when he used that word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not the general would be able to answer the question, the Chamber will not be assisted very much. Why don't we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 65 ter 12397.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there armed incidents involving UNPROFOR and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? How did you react in those cases?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was just one clash with members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I wouldn't be able to say that it was actually a clash with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The people involved were paramilitaries, members of a paramilitary army. And I had a lot of problems subsequently. I later on resubordinated those people to the Ilijas Brigade and they started behaving. I believe that you are asking me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any other conflicts involving UNPROFOR in any of our zones of responsibilities. Really, we did not have any such problems with UNPROFOR. There were minor things but not such problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it says around at 10.25 they opened fire on our positions. Can we go to the following page. Your memory serves you well, General, sir. It seems that UNPROFOR and [indiscernible], that there was no love lost between them. Under 7 it says that Vasilije Vidovic, Vasko was slightly wounded. Is that the person that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned Vasko and that was at the time. Vasilije Vidovic, also known as Vasko, was a member of the paramilitary in the territory of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. We had a vojvoda there. Actually, we had three --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Besides sending protests, you did not use weapons in response to their activities; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, too fast. Too fast. I'm not sure if your question was correctly translated or reflected in the transcript. Probably we need to hear the answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, also -- from the moment when you said also known as Vasko whom you resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and that you did not have any conflicts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's slightly different but in essence it's the same. I resubordinated him to the Ilijas Brigade, not to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, because if I'd done that I would have resubordinated him directly to me. He hailed from Ilijas, from Podogovo [phoen]. He behaved the way he did and that's why we had to resubordinate him to the unit up there. The question was whether we responded or reacted to UNPROFOR activities. We did not. The only thing we did is send protests and whatever misunderstandings we may have had we resolved with UNPROFOR. Actually, there was an incident involving a vehicle. Somebody stole a vehicle, and that's how the problem arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3472, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did it arrive that NATO aircraft caused an incident and opened fire against our army?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information to the effect that fire was opened in an area, and later on we could not check whether that was true or not. There were provocations, mostly by NATO aircraft, that patrolled the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There were up to 150 sorties a day which depended on the situation and on the weather. When they broke the sound barrier, that instilled fear among the troops and the people because it was not a pleasant sound to hear that. And you were just hopeless. You couldn't do anything because you could not open fire on such aircraft. Even if we had had the -- the carte blanche to do it, we did not have the means to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D01562.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be reminded that he should speak slowly. Otherwise, his words cannot recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. General Galic, I understand you have a lot of things to -- to let us know, but in doing so, please speak very slowly. Otherwise, your words will not be recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have been in detention for 14 years, so probably you should try and understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at bullets 5 and 6. It says at 1500 hours two NATO pact aircraft flew over the positions above Cekrcici very low about 150 to 200 metres. Fire was opened but there were no consequences. So what did you do about this? You just lodged a protest with the UNPROFOR; is that right? It says here: "Protest Lodged with UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that first of all the Chamber needs to be informed about the location of Cekrcici. It's quite a small area. That was where a check-point was from Visoko leading towards Ilijas and our check-point was in operation there. If something happened in that area or if there was firing there, it wasn't so dangerous or did not have such an impact on the disposition of other forces because other forces of our corps were deployed elsewhere. That was why just a protest was lodged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3473, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were your protests lodged with UNPROFOR fruitful in any way? Did they result in anything advantage to us. Did UNPROFOR have an influence on the opposing side as it had an influence on you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question for me, now -- or, rather, not the question itself but the answer. For me to compare whether they had equal or more or less influence on the other side. But what they presented to us as the measures taken against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps beginning from the implementation of the agreement that we talked about, that is to say the exclusion zone, without heavy weapons. I know that everyone came to check and monitor that agreement, from Mr. Akashi to the commander from Zagreb. I mean, the UNPROFOR commander. But we know that the agreement was not implemented on the Muslim side and there were not so many checks. That's why we could say that we were not equally treated by the UN representatives in general, not just UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D06330.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date of this document is the 28th of February, 1994; that is to say, after the Markale I incident. And what the document says is that the enemy continues not to observe the agreed truce. And under item 2: "Our units all observed the signed truce." But can we please see the last page or the second one, rather. It could be the last page in English because the items I'm interested in are 8 and 10.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please look at this number 8. "The Muslims continue to breach the cease-fire with engineering work," and so on. And the last one, conclusions, the measures which the UNPROFOR is taking after our protests have yielded no results so that lodging further protests has no purpose.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, this is my signature. So no "poturice" are mentioned here but rather just the Muslims. This is why I wanted to go back to the explanation I provided earlier. Whether measures were taken, I'm warning the Main Staff here that they are not taking sufficient measures against the 1st Corps of the BH Army. Perhaps it's a bit severely formulated that there is no purpose to continue lodging protests. I was probably somewhat angry at the time. Something else was going on in the zone of the corps and this was not going well. You keep writing protests and no results. So that was why I wrote it the way I did. Perhaps it was a bit too strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is a MOS violation, General? In point 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That stands for Muslim forces. Muslim armed forces, to be precise. The Muslim armed forces, MOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3474, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01667 is the one we need to look at now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for it to appear on the screen, the Presiding Judge asked me about the MOS. It is good to see here that these forces, the Muslim air forces [as interpreted], were crossing from Dobrinja towards Igman across the airport where it says MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The date of this document is the 1st of March 1993. You are saying where the enemy carried out its activities. Under item 1, fire at Nedzarici. The faculty of transportation. And under item 3, the situation in the territory, you say that a meeting was held between you and General Soubirou and that you protested because the truce agreement was violated by firing sniper fire, regrouping of forces, engineering works carried out by the Muslim army. Were these activities allowed when a truce was in force? Just tell us briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please see the last page of this document. It -- the manners in which the truce was violated are listed here and you say in particular in the vicinity of the UNPROFOR units which are carrying out checks or monitoring in specific sectors. Last sentence: "Meetings and agreements with the UN commander are not producing the anticipated results, particularly with regard to the -- respecting the cease-fire." So you were not satisfied with what you could achieve by protests; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is all in the context of the agreement which had you signed with Mr. Akashi on the 18th of February, 1994. As far as I can see this is the date, and I had missed it. So this is -- continues all this time that agreement on the cessation of firing in the entire Sarajevo zone was still in force. That covers the entire 20-kilometre zone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D06329 is the one we would need now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the date is now the 24th of March, 1994. UNPROFOR activities is a separate section. We should have the translation too. We have seen the date. Perhaps we can scroll down. What is described here is a series of measures and counter-measures with regard to disagreements, objections. They are trying to justify what they had omitted to do and once again the problems are listed here. No translation. If you could then please tell us. It says here that all the problems were stressed again. They were the subjects of discussion earlier but they have not been resolved. Can you please read out what is mentioned under item 1 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say what the introductory section says. It says that the UNPROFOR refused to transport me across the airport. They wanted to retaliate in a way because we did not meet some of their demands. They wanted to patrol in the Vogosca sector. What was that about? When I needed to go to the north western section of the front, and that was Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas, and that part of the front, if I were to take the Lukavica-Pale-Sumbulovac-Hresa-Vogosca road, from Sumbulovac towards Hresa, that section that was a path for horses, and I didn't want to go there at all I would mean between four and six hours depending on the enemy fire, and if I was transported by UNPROFOR, I would cross the entire way from Lukavica to Ilidza in 10 to 15 minutes. That was why I used that opportunity whenever I had it, whenever they would provide me with their APC and place it at my disposal so that I could do my job. The other issues that we discussed which had not been resolved, first: The return of Muslims to the agreed line on Igman and Bjelasnica. Do I need to provide explanations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber knows when you acceded those positions.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2, preventing the Muslim movements below and across the airport. Number 3, monitoring the truce by preventing the movements of Muslim forces, firing, and engineering works. Perhaps it's not clear, those engineering works and what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Violations of agreement with regard to the deployment of the Russian unit in the general Grbavica area. What is meant here is actually Debelo Brdo though it's not written that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just didn't understand how Dr. Karadzic could say the Chamber is aware of that when none of us are and we can't read the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Chamber already knows what engineering works are in the military sense of the word, and I believe that it does. It means digging trenches, bunkers, getting closer to positions, and I believe that the Chamber is aware of this. So we shouldn't waste any time on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 5, the use of caterpillars and weapons with calibre higher than 12.7-millimetres. That is prohibited. Under 6, continuing flights of UN helicopters above our positions counter to the agreement. Movement of UN vehicles and personnel without announcement and approval. That's under number 7. Number 8, transportation of Muslims in UN vehicles. That's what this page contains. I'm not certain if there's anything on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the following page to see what else you objected to. On top of the page you say regardless of the existence of the series of unresolved problems, six military observers persisted in trying to shift the discussion to the issue of patrols along the front line. And below, under item 8, conclusions, expectations, you note that the enemy is continuing to violate the truce. Further provocations are to be expected and so on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Though it says on top of the page what was emphasised was a major incident when the Canadians violently entered our positions in the general Cekrcici area or sector. That was the incident which I talked about previously and it is now confirmed in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06315, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There should be a translation. General, do you remember that you also addressed the government with the information you had received about the burial and removal of the bodies of Serb civilians who had been killed in Sarajevo and that you requested that the government block such manipulation with the bodies through UNPROFOR. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen that I signed this document, and now that I'm reading it, I can remember what that was about in the particular period. The essence was that we had received information from those who had crossed over to our territory and also through our observation and reconnaissance and intelligence that bodies of those who had been killed or wounded were being moved. We did not know who that was, whether these were Serbs' bodies, but most information was that the Serbs' bodies were moved and buried under those who had already been buried at the cemetery under other bodies so that it could not be seen where that was done. Much information with regard to this. And, therefore, I had to send it to the Main Staff for their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? And then we could take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3477, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break for a half an hour and resume at 11.00 -- oh, no, I'm sorry. We'll break for an hour and resume at 11.30. Would that be sufficient, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour. And I thank you very much for that accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to move on to another topic, and that's our internal functioning and the co-ordination and compatibility between the civilian and military components of the commands. How did you perceive that command process? Can you explain to the Chamber the difference between the Main Staff and the General Staff? How did -- how did it work? And let us remain at the highest level, the level of the republic, and not go down to the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the RS, there was the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. That command was headed by you. There was also the Main Staff of the VRS, headed by the commander of the Main Staff, and that was General Mladic. It was customary for the Supreme Command to have its own staff, rather than having a separate Main Staff. That's based on the experience from the Second World War in former Yugoslavia. It was necessary at the time because communication lines did not function, and that's when the commanders of the Main Staffs, republic or republic [as interpreted] were appointed, and that was communicated to the forces who had to obey them. I don't know to what extent the RS needed a Main Staff. To my mind, an organisational and formational problem arose due to that because there was the Supreme Command and the Supreme Commander who were to command the armed forces including the army of Republika Srpska, all of it. And now, there was the commander of the Main Staff who was not the commander of the army. He was appointed by the National Assembly of the RS. And his real position was commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska rather than commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Thus, the problem of the relations with subordinate commands arose. There was a kind of a parallel commanding or dual commanding. In Sarajevo, I had a lot of commands commanding me. I'll give you an example. The supreme commander, President Karadzic commanded me. So did General Mladic as commander of the Main Staff, he also issued orders. Sector commanders also -- UNPROFOR sector commanders also commanded. They implemented some Resolutions of the Security Council. They were authorised to control some things and so on. So there were a number of lines of command, and I had to adapt to that. The relationship between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff should have been for the Main Staff to be the staff of the Supreme Command, and it should have done or should have worked the way -- in the way that was provided for in the laws and regulations, and the commander of the Main Staff should have only commanded the army to the extent as transferred to him by the Supreme Commander. As far as I know, this authority mostly referred to organisational and formational changes, although the appointment of command was in the remit of the Supreme Commander. The commander of the Main Staff was not able to do it. The Supreme Command could also directly command corps; that is, the corps commanders, but he could also command by way of the Main Staff. Most of the combat activities were only commanded by the Supreme Commander in principle through his directives, whereas it was the Main Staff that drafted the directives to the subordinate command and they were also signed by the commander of the Main Staff. So there was a bit of confusion. Who was it that actually commanded the army? Was it the Supreme Commander or the commander of the Main Staff? This duality was not so -- so much felt at the beginning, because there were lots of other problems to take care of, but it was understandable that the Supreme Command had to transfer some tasks and obligations to the commander of the Main Staff because the Supreme Commander was also president of the republic and party president and he has a lot of work both internally and internationally, so he had to transfer some of his authority to someone to command the army. There was also the minister of the interior who commanded the MUP, and on the other hand there was also the commander the Main Staff who could exercise the authority transferred to him. I could go on speaking about the organisation and commanding at the level of the Supreme Command but that would take hours and hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Of the three levels of commanding, strategic, operational, and tactical, to your mind what was still exercised by the Supreme Commander, that is the president of the republic, and what did he transfer to the Main Staff through his decision on formation and organisation dated 15 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not all that familiar with the content of that decision because that -- that's above my level. There was communication between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff. But basically, planning and conduct of combat activity was mostly transferred to the Main Staff so they were supposed to make these plans and the commander of the Main Staff was authorised to sign these. You didn't deal with these things much, but I'm sure that you exercised some sort of control. To what extent, I don't know. There was also the Ministry of Defence, which had its duties with regard to the army, especially when it comes to manning, materiel and technical equipment, ammunition, and so on. All plans about manning, organisation, and formations were, to a great extent, transferred to the Main Staff. I suppose that they briefed you about their solutions to some problems, but basically those powers were transferred to them. They were delegated. I think this is it enough for a corps commander to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now, General, sir, when it comes to the operative orders that I sent to you, except for those that arose from my agreements with Akashi or, for example, the agreement that was signed in Geneva with regard to humanitarian work or with regard to some cease-fires, did you ever receive from me an operative order to do one or the other thing, to take one or the other area? Did you ever receive any operative commands or orders from me directly?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was very good, but my answer was not -- my previous answer was not as good as that. The strategical level of command was at the level of the Supreme Command and the Main Staff. The operative level was at the level of the corps. The tactical level actually was subdivided into two different levels, into basic tactical units and joint tactical units. Basic tactical units were up to the size of a battalion. From battalion upwards, those units were the so-called joint tactical units, though a division was the largest tactical unit, whereas a corps was an operative unit. I believe that I've said enough about that level. And now I would like to answer your last question as to whether I ever received any orders about a direct use of units in combat. While I was in charge, I don't remember any such orders that arrived at the corps. Whether you sent any or not, you should answer that. I don't think so. If you did, then it was -- it was done through the Main Staff. Some orders and directives went through the Main Staff to us, to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if something like that happened would the Main Staff have evoked my direct order or my agreement with somebody in the preamble? Did you receive information that it was at my request?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we had a document before us in this courtroom where I did evoke an order of the Supreme Command and the Main Staff. Whether they did the same in the Main Staff, whether they referred your document and agreements that you signed, I don't know. But I remember that particular document, and I drew your attention to the fact that the main commander the Supreme Command was cited. They referred you, and I had to evoke the authority of a superior command because sometimes it's very good, especially in war time, to evoke a higher authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what authority did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the authority of the commander of the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander. Because the Supreme Commander had the authority. Of course, he did. There's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at first there were no tensions and misunderstandings. How did you perceive those misunderstandings once they arose? Were -- were those misunderstandings result of some crimes or did they have some other conceptual or ideological background?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to an ideological background, I don't think that they had any such thing. It's very difficult for me to say anything about the relationship between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff -- command. However, as far as I could tell, at a lower level, there were no such misunderstandings. At first, we were referred to as Tito's officers, and then I remember that I was in Ilidza and I said I never sported Tito's kerchief around the neck and you may have. I don't know. But things were done gradually. We sorted out and ironed out our difference gradually. At the level of the plan as to what needed to be done, which also was tantamount to the three strategic and operative plan, it seems to me that if I saw the things well, the first conflict arose while you were in Geneva. An agreement should have been signed and at that time we were involved in an operation, Vukovar [as interpreted] 93. That was in the month of August 1993, namely. Some of the orders that arrived at that time, I don't know whether they were in compliance with what you had regulated and what you had said before the beginning of the operation itself and your departure for Geneva. I think that things were done differently and that they were not in keeping with what you wanted. If my memory serves me well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to make an alteration in the transcript. It was not Vukovar 93 but Lukavac 93. I would like to ask witness to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar is in Croatia and Lukavac, of course, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, yes, I said Lukavac, not Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic asked you about the difference between Main Staff and General Staff. I -- I think you explained, in detail, about the Main Staff, but I don't think we heard about General Staff. If you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we did not have a General Staff. I skipped that part. We had only a Main Staff. In all militaries, a General Staff is, indeed, set up, and that staff in war time becomes the staff of the Supreme Command. It has the chief of the then General Staff. It doesn't have a commander. There are many other organisational and establishment differences, but the main difference would lie in that. Those staffs have Chiefs of Staff. They don't have commanders. In all the militaries worldwide, that would be the situation. If you need any more details, I can provide them, but I believe that it -- when it comes to Republika Srpska, no further details are necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At one point of time after the war, was the Main Staff transformed into a General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, it became a General Staff, yes. I don't know when that happened, but, yes, it did become the General Staff of the VRS. It was no longer its Main Staff. I believe that they moved to Bijeljina. It became the General Staff. I was retired already. I was pensioned off in 1994. So I was no longer with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure that the answer given by the witness at the end of page 38, line 25, is completely accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose so because General Mladic -- General Galic said that as far as it is concerned with Republika Srpska, that would be insufficient [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can understand the context. Let's continue. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell the Trial Chamber something about the difference between the General Staff and the staff of the Supreme Command or rather between the Main Staff and the command of the -- Supreme Command in terms of the influence and activities of the Supreme Commander. Is there any difference? And if there is, what does it consist of?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the organisation and establishment, except for the name there is no other important difference because it is a staff. Both are the staffs that work for the Supreme Command. The Main Staff has a commander who has been authorised by the Supreme Command to do certain things and he can command the staff where there's no other commander. He does staff work. He has a Chief of Staff. He doesn't have a commander, and he directly carries out orders given to me -- to him by the Supreme Commander, i.e., the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you spoke too fast, so it seems here according to the transcript that the Main Staff carries out staff work.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both staffs carry out staff tasks. Both the General Staff and the Main Staff. However, General Staff does not have a commander. It has a chief. Certain authorities and obligations can be transferred to that staff by the Supreme Commander as well. However, in the Main Staff we have a commander. As soon as you have a commander, that commander has higher and wider authorities than a chief. He can make decisions, issue orders, in a different way than a chief can. Have I been clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Can you tell us, to the extent you know about my letters being sent to the corps level, to what extent did those letters concern operations or aborting operations and to what extent they concern humanitarian aid? Can you please tell the Trial Chamber on what occasions did I address certain corps and tackled certain issues with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He's done it a few times now and I haven't risen, but when Dr. Karadzic -- when Dr. Karadzic asked the question at page 41 about the extent what the General knows about particular types of his letters, he was starting to lead the General. And perhaps he should be reminded not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic can reformulate his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that we clarified that. The General confirmed that he did not receive any executive orders from me, but I know that I did send letters. I'm asking the General what were those letters about. If those were not executive orders, what were those letters sent to his corps contain?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I can remember, there were no immediate combat orders. I did receive any such thing from the Supreme Command. I received them from the Main Staff. You addressed us on several occasions with regard to humanitarian issues and with regard to the implementation of some agreements; for example, all those agreements that you helped sign, including the agreement that we have just discussed, TEZ [Realtime transcript read in error "DTEZ"]. I participated at that and with this regard I received an order. But most of the issues concerned humanitarian aid and dealing with situations and issues. There were no any other matters because the -- those matters were resolved by orders and directives by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On line 1, the TEZ should stand for the Total Exclusion Zone. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber something about Lukavac 93. What did that operation entail in geographical terms? What crisis do you have in mind when you say -- because Lukavac 93 was a code-name and there was another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down. "DTEZ" should read the "TEZ," which means Total Exclusion Zone. So line 6 so reflect that as well. Please slow down. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, instead of Lukavac 93, could you explain the events without using the code-name?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. I will gladly explain that part. This was an operation by the Army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Apologise for interrupting the General, but it's Lukavac, 93, not Lukavica 93.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lukavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about that on day one. Is there any other term that could be applied to that event without using the code-name? Where did the operation take place and what was its outcome?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army the code-names are customary. It's nothing new. But it took place in Jahorina, Trnovo, Hojita [phoen], Igman, Bjelasnica. On the other side there were auxiliary axis, Hadzici, Igman, Trsevo [phoen] Brdo, the next auxiliary axis from which the Herzegovina Corps was advancing is the Rogoj pass in the direction of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the agreement? What did that agreement refer to that was signed after that operation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen that agreement. General Milovanovic came to me together with my operative Cedo Sladoje. They informed me that I had to withdraw from that area, the area of mounts Bjelasnica and Igman, to an area - and that was sometime on the 14th of August, 1993 - to an area where I had been on the 31st of July of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And what about the area where you were at the time? You withdrew from that area. Who did you leave it to?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with my forces and the other combined forces, because I had been reinforced from forces from the other corps, I withdrew some 27 kilometres away from that area that we had reached before then. And that area of Mount Bjelasnica and Mount Igman was taken -- handed over to UNPROFOR. I have already told you about the problems that we encountered during our withdrawal towards Hadzici and the area of Tresno [phoen] Brdo and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who did you hand the area over to according to my agreement from Geneva?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible to catch up with the speed. It's simply impossible to catch up with the speed. Please slow down and put a pause. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now asking the General this: We are talking about the relationship between the civilian commands and the military commands and I would like to ask him to be as brief as possible in his answers because I want to finish eventually. You have just mentioned that I addressed the corps with regard to humanitarian issues. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what my position was and what you received from me with regard to letting the convoys through and the flow of humanitarian aid for the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, from you and from the commander of the Main Staff, I received orders according to which I was supposed to comply with everything that had been agreed. The -- the direction of movement of those convoys, who had the right to stop and control them, or they were sometimes even not controlled and they would be allowed to go directly to the area under the control of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army in Sarajevo. If a major problem arose, such was the problem with arms having been found in those convoys, then we reported the incidents to the Main Staff. I don't know and I don't remember whether you issued anything about -- with that regard, but I'm sure that you were abreast of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Having in mind our command structure, if you received different instructions from me and Mladic, which ones were you supposed to follow?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. But let me tell you this. In terms of subordination and the principle of unity of command, it is something that is part of every military organisation. Only one person is in command. The other principle is that a superior's order must be obeyed. In this situation my immediate superior to me, who issued different orders and who had influence in terms of other aspects was General Mladic. Let me remind you. Perhaps this would not be the best way to formulate it, but when in August 1995 you removed General Mladic, he rallied all of the generals in place at the time who signed a letter declaring their loyalty to him. And, in the end, you had to withdraw that order. That's to my recollection because I had already been retired by the time. I remember us being together in Banski Dvori when civilians were being pulled out of Drvar. I suppose you recall that. At the time, the situation was critical in that part of Krajina because between 14 and 17 municipalities were lost. Of course, people were upset with many things as well as with Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic. I don't know about the extent but it was not very safe in the area of Krajina. I went to see him in Banski Dvori which also served as part -- for the forward command post of the Supreme Command. At the time, he tried to establish contact with the Main Staff, asking for Mladic and others, but was unsuccessful because no one responded for reasons unbeknownst to me. I know the problem at the time was when the civilians would pull out of Drvar and whether our army was there. In that area, the Croatian army had carried out an attack and there was a danger for the civilians facing the fate they were not supposed to. I recall your decision at the time and the hardship you had in terms of reaching an agreement with the municipal president whom I had known from before. You had to agree with him on what would be done and when and in what way civilians would leave Drvar. That is how I could see that something was not quite working right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, how did you see this attempt of mine from August 1995 to have the Main Staff changed to the Supreme Command staff? What were my reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- it is the Sanski Most meeting, as far as I can recall. By doing that, you wanted to have the Main Staff changed to the General Staff so as to have it directly subordinated to you and so that there would be no question in terms of who was commanding the army. I think that was your focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber about Banski Dvori. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to another topic which is the issue of supply of Sarajevo, in terms of electricity water and gas. Please tell us where most of the water came to Sarajevo -- where from it came, who was in control of the sources and what it depended on whether the town would have water or not. Was it our army that turned the tap off, or were there other reasons in place due to which the supply of water was made impossible?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at a map, any geographical map, you will see where the water pipelines are. The sources of water, for the most part, were in the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There were sources of water inside Sarajevo, too, but they were far smaller. The biggest problem regarding that issue was dealt with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Muratovic. They discussed the supply of gas, electricity, and water. In the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, we always wanted to meet all of their obligations. The supply of water was directly dependant on the supply of electricity. If there was electricity, the pumps could be working in order to achieve pressure.
