If there was no electricity, the problem was great. We knew that only the natural flow could be used to supply water to Sarajevo. In such circumstance in both parts of Sarajevo, in the area controlled by the 1st Corps of ABiH and the SRK, there were many high-rise buildings in those areas which required greater pressure which could not be achieved without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us about the water supply from Bistrica and Tilava and other mountain sources such as Mostanica, could they reach Sarajevo by free-fall or -- and did you ever prevent that kind of water supply from such sources that did not require electricity?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was never a manipulation in terms of water supply. There was never any abuse of water supply in order to have someone sanctioned or punished by doing so. It is impossible to stop the flow of water because one creates a dam which then, in turn, may be very dangerous. On the other hand, the territory and the pipeline system was intertwined. For example, if in the area of Bistrik there was no water, there was no water in Grbavica, and Grbavica was held by the SRK. If I -- I seem to recall that with the aid of UNPROFOR in the area of Bacevac [phoen], which is Ilidza, we built a separate reservoir to supply water to the area controlled by the ABiH 1st Corps. If you were to ask me about the capacity of that tank, I'd say I don't know about it but I know it was constructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bacevo was in Ilidza. What was the level -- or actually what was the importance of Bacevo and was it also dependant on electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bacevo is lower down. If we take into account the laws of physics, it did require electricity in order to be able to use the reservoirs in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, while you were in command of the corps, the SRK, were there any epidemics in the Muslim-held part?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a very interesting question. Neither in the Muslim nor in the SRK part in Sarajevo there were no epidemics as far as I know. Imagine, even though people already lived under difficult conditions because occasionally there wasn't any water or food, the rate of morbidity was low. Even when there were greater problems. For example, I was at Bjelasnica in winter-time, people did not fall ill. It's a miracle. I have no other explanation. I'm not an expert. But there must have been something that nature took upon itself to take care of the people in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D06306.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is dated the 10th of November --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Mr. Karadzic probably meant October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- 1992. You are in command at the time. Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it is the 14th of October in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: October. Apologies, if I am mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph from the bottom that has to do with water, electricity, gas, and postal services. We see in item 10 that there was a conversation with General Razek and Magnusson. You discussed water and electricity. So what was concluded? You say here the issue of water, electricity, and gas, we said that our side had done everything to achieve this but that the same should be applied to the other areas of Republika Srpska. Did you ever put in place any conditions, and did they provide the same thing for the Krajina that you did for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not put any conditions in place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic repeatedly leads the witness and, with respect, I would ask that he be firmly cautioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we discussed this issue of water supply before, but I couldn't find the passage in the document and what -- I don't remember what the point was. Now I understand you are pushing hard to conclude as soon as possible but, to the contrary, it ruins the probative value of the witness. Please take your time in putting the question correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to check the translation first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But given the fact that in the report we see that the Serb side was ready to implement everything but, it says, we mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is leading, that comment of yours. Just put the passage and ask the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the third or fourth paragraph done deals with water and electricity. Please explain your position with regard to that and do point out whether this was imposing a condition or merely a request to be treated equally.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the representative for civilian affairs was here - I forget his name - for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he agreed, we accepted all demands and stated that we would do whatever necessary to make possible water, electricity, and gas supply. But we also said that this should be done elsewhere as well in other parts of Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. By "elsewhere," what -- what did you mean? It says in English translation: "The same should be applied to other areas of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report says that we supported everything that was demanded with regard to water, electricity, and gas supply in Sarajevo, and that this was the way it should be like in all of Republika Srpska. There were some towns in the RS - I don't remember which exactly - that depend on the sources controlled by the BH Army, and those towns had no water supply or electricity supply. But I can't be more precise than that. We didn't put conditions, but what this is about is taking measures to make possible such supply everywhere. I don't think it's a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01177, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, take a look at the fourth paragraph from the top. The one starting with: "Around 1445 hours..." Why is this important?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shells were launched from 120-millimetre mortars of the BH Army and the transformer station in Blazuj somewhere was hit. Here it says that four tonnes of fuel leaked. But it isn't fuel; it's oil. That transformer station at Blazuj was extremely important because it was a switch for Ilidza and Vogosca, as far as I remember. The power lines. I'm sure that experts know better than I. But the transformer station was hit. And then reaction was, well, there is no electricity and there's no water. Of course there isn't. There is no electricity the pumps can't work and there is no public lighting. Of course, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did that reflect on the pumps at Bacevo and the water supply in the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know where exactly the power line ran, but I suppose that it affected that area because one branch went from Jablanica and Konjic descending to Hrasnica, referring to a power line, and possibly it's important for the area you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get 1D01445, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the procedure for the repair of electric installations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were joint commissions. As far as I remember, I don't want to read these documents because I know what was done, although I don't know the details. There were commissions that met. They were joint commissions with members from both sides. And then the time and place were agreed on, and what should be done by whom. And the commands would be informed that no fire should be opened at that place as long as the power line or the water-pipe line or whatever it was were repaired. This is it basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second sentence in the first paragraph. It says: "The enemy is taking advantage of the suspension fire" -- Your fire is meant, right? Read it: "The enemy is taking advantage of the suspension of fire in the area where repairs are being carried out on the power transmission line and is firing on our positions from the immediate vicinity of the area where repairs are being carried out. If enemy fire is neutralised, our side is blamed." Do explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an agreement is reached that fire should ceased from both sides, then the enemy takes advantage of that cease-fire and moves in the area where these repairs are carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if you do respond?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we do, then the agreement is null and void and no repairs will be carried out on either side. There will be conflict which will again result in a new meeting and a new agreement about repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this sentence: "From the immediate vicinity of the area where repairs are being carried out." If you were to respond, then you would have been accused; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must understand this tactics. I don't know if there was an opportunity for our forces to take advantage of that. I don't think that they ever did because the agreement was that no combat activity should be carried out in a certain area. And then they would move their forces, hiding behind this safe zone. If a decision is taken to respond, then all unwanted consequences would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D01552.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us. This is dated the 19th of June, 1993. The second paragraph of item 1 reads: "At 1720 hours and 1740 hours the enemy fired shells and rifle grenades on the cargo gate and power line near Pretis. The latter was damaged and Pretis could not work due to a power outage. Sniping at Vogosca," and so on. Tell us, if the state of affairs with the power line at Vogosca affected Velesici in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is said here that this part of the power line targeted was damaged. It runs parallel to the front line and enters Vogosca and continues toward the centre of Sarajevo, but I don't have a map to be able to say where exactly those power lines ran. But I'm sure that they go to the centre of the city because one line ran from Hadzici, another from Vogosca, and one part from Pale down to the old city. The power line went through the area of the 1st Corps of the BH Army and only then would it reach the area of the SRK, whereas the lines from Igman and Hrasnica originated at Jablanica and up to July they had a hydroelectric power plant on the Zeljeznica river. These are the lines I know that were used to supply Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 15595. The 15th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, on that day you issued an order for the unobstructed passage for humanitarian aid. The order was sent to all units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, General. In the preamble you refer to my directive. It says -- or rather, would you read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order: "For the unobstructed passage of humanitarian aid to be sent to all units of the SRK. Based on the directive of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential 01-87-1/93, of 14 May 1993, the order of the Main Staff of the VRS, strictly confidential number" -- this is illegible. I'll skip it. "Also of the 14th of May, 1993. In order to keep the signed truce from -- on our side and the consistent implementation of the directive, I order the following: "Make possible the unobstructed passage and protection of packages, equipment, and personnel that provides aid to the civilian population of the opposing side. "Second, ban the misuse of foodstuffs, crops, water installations, and drinking water supplies for military purposes. This also included dams at hydro power plants."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do continue. This is also important.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Third, fully adhere to the Geneva Conventions for the protection of the victims of war of 12 August," I suppose, "1949."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So General, I issued a directive on the 14th and the Main Staff issued an order on the 14th, and on the 15th you already sent it out. Did it reach all units and did you demand that this be respected?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in the heading "to all units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." And this order was complied with. I don't think that anything was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3482, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let us now deal with the issue of command and control, discipline and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'd like to see 1D07524.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Immediately after you took over command, you probably made a snap-shot of the situation. And now let's see what the measures were to correct shortcomings. Take a look at this document and tell us what you ordered. Actually, at the first page there's a description of the existing state affairs and what you object to, and on the following page there is your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When Dr. Karadzic tells the witness, Let's see what the measures are to correct shortcomings, he's leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the document is self-explanatory. I thought it was clear. It's a document drafted and signed by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you introduce this document to us without reading? What prompted you to issue this document a week or two after taking command.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the font is so small that I can't read anything, so I can only speak from memory to the extent I can remember things now. But basically the situation I found was such that there was neither a corps commander nor a Chief of Staff at the corps. General Sipcic had left the corps about a month before I arrived. Maybe even two months. And they left the command post with part of the Command Staff. At that time the airport was surrendered, and in the north-west of the front line there is a lack of discipline and many unresolved issues, that's the area of Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas, Vogosca, and Rajlovac. At the portion where the 1st Sarajevo Brigade and 2nd Sarajevo Brigade were and the corps command toured Kijevo, Kasindol, and Jahorina, when I arrived the front line ran through Jahorina. In this section toward the end of the Jug 92 operation conducted by the BH Army, they cut off Herzegovina from the remainder of the RS. So we were unable to communicate, and they were exerting constant pressure on Lukavica and the -- those forces of the corps that were there. Then the authorities. The situation was such that the JNA had left and TO units were left behind but they had not yet sufficiently been incorporated into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. This all helps. However, please pay attention to the paragraphs describing what you found looting, lack of discipline. Look at the first page. Look at those paragraphs where all that is described. There's a reference to crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe Dr. Karadzic could ask for the B/C/S version to be enlarged so that the General could read it. Because the General said that he can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it -- it -- after that moment, the font will enlarge a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now the font is good. The letters have been blown up and now I can read the document, whereas I couldn't do it before. I spoke only from memory and you know those things happened 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please do not read aloud. Just cast a glance at the document and then tell us what you found, what you established, and then we will move onto the following page and we will see what you ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. This is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With this regard, I have encountered different forms of looting, robbery, and all sorts of criminal behaviour, as well as all the other forms of acquisition of material gain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in your own words, rephrase. You don't need to read.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that there are all sorts of evils that were caused by war and they are all mentioned here: Looting, robbery, acquiring material gain, because we're talking about property that had to be taken over. The authorities were still not in place and they were not doing their job. That's for sure. It says furthermore that many thought that was a period during which they could amass a large wealth, so -- and we know there was a lot of looting everywhere and that was also present in this area. I'm saying here that while some people were waging war, the others are making the most of it -- the situation in order to amass wealth and that caused dissatisfaction among people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the order part of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the English page be displayed for the benefit of the English-speaking participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the bullet point 3 where you say that -- use all means to prevent looting, thieving, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 3. I'm interested in bullet point 6 of this order. For the benefit of the English-speaking participants in the trial, bullet point 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under 6, you say: "I forbid the movement of civilian vehicles in combat areas. I also ban gathering of civilians in organised or unorganized manners." Tell me, please, did the other side, the opposing side honour that and apply that to their civilians? Was that an obligation that should have been complied with on both sides?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was my assessment that we had to regulate that part of combat activities about 5 kilometres in depth. That some sort of order had to be established, as it were, in order to prevent unnecessary losses among civilians. One of those measures was to ban people from loitering at bus-stops, that humanitarian aid was not distributed in open area, that if water had to be distributed, it had to be done in shelters or in basements, not in open spaces, that buildings and other facilities had to be protected from the enemy fire. The other side, the opposing side, as far as I know, and when I remember the incidents that we discussed, I realised that they did not take all those measures. In the Additional Protocol number I regulates the obligations of the civilian protection. According to that protocol, the civilian protection should regulate all those issued and it should demand from the civilian population to behave in keeping with the decisions of the command and the civilian protection. I don't know what measures they took. I am not in a position to know. However, in view of the consequences I can tell that they did not do enough. I don't know how much they could do together with UNPROFOR in terms of the protection of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06324. Could you please remind me when our next break is? I would like to finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going to take a break at 1.00 for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll do our best to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, take a look at the document which was issued on the 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not pressing you. It's for you to decide how to spend your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, thank you. But I have some precious witnesses that I need to lead live, so I'm wondering whether I'll have enough time left to call all the witnesses that I have planned, so I'm trying to economise, or if you were to give me some additional time, I wouldn't be facing that problem at all. If you gave me an additional couple of hours for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please look at the letter that was sent on the 22nd of May, 1993, to all brigades, regiments, and independent units. You report or, rather, you inform and the document was signed by Sladoje on your behalf, and it was about what happened at the assembly on the 19th of May, 1993. Please -- I'm drawing your attention to some criticism that was addressed at the -- in military with regard to discipline and order.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was a joint meeting with the government and the Supreme Command as well as the Main Staff, if I'm not mistaken. And on that occasion, the representatives of the government put forth some problems that the Army of Republika Srpska was riddled with. And that included the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There was a lot of criticism. And that was an assembly meeting, not just a -- any meeting. It was a meeting of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. There was a lot of criticism about alcoholism, looting, thieving, lack of discipline, failure to respond to call-ups. It was said that both order and discipline had to be stepped up and my order followed that criticism. The way I interpreted things was this: If there was an internal order and discipline, everything else will follow. It will be easy to regulate other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 you demand rigorous measures to applied against those who abused weapons, looted, and you demanded that they be punished by court-martial. Under 2 you put a ban on the organisation of any paramilitaries, parapolice units, and parapolitical groups on the part of individuals or group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to this part of my work, I can say that a lot was done at the corps level in order to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page, bullet point 2, in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in Serbian, the following page, bullet point 3, where it says: "I strictly forbid any involvement by all levels of command and control in the affairs of the local authorities."

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And vice versa. The authorities should not interfere with the issues of army command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06314, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of June, 1993, you noticed that there were a lot of informal groups in the zones of responsibility and that those groups instill fear among civilians and they bring uncertainty among the soldiers. And it says these informal groups also use arms, that they don't refrain from that. What civilian population was being disturbed? Was there any special group or did they disturb everybody irrespective of their religious affiliations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those informal group, that was a time when the corps had already dealt with paramilitaries and other informal groups that existed in the zone of responsibility of the corps. First and foremost, those groups disturbed peace among the population irrespective of their religious affiliation. Criminals did not choose their targets along those lines. They exercised their intentions irrespective of the affiliations of their target group. At that time we had a lot of negative occurrences in the north western part of our zone of responsibility, and there were strifes for that area to become independent by way of establishing a Chetnik corps. There was a lack of discipline and excessive use of all sorts of equipment, and that's why I was of the opinion that a commander of the Igman Brigade had to be removed from his position. At that time we disbanded Brna's [phoen] group that was in the orchard. It was another informal group that did not carry out its orders and tasks. It actually bothered both the authorities and civilians in the area. That group was disbanded and its members were attached to various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3485, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06316 is the document that I'm looking for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it, General, sir, Brna's group, which you mentioned, did you recruit into your units those people who had committed crimes and used to belong to that group?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that group --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's another leading question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I beg to differ, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we -- shall he continue or, Ms. Edgerton, could you explain a bit further? Or can I hear from Mr. Robinson first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It doesn't suggest an answer. The leading question -- definition of a leading question is a question which suggests an answer. This one doesn't suggest an answer. It could be answered yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please answer, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not recruit individuals who had committed crimes. They were then handed over to courts and prosecutor's offices and military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the document which was issued on the 31st of May, 1994. You reported to the Main Staff that you had informed the brigade commanders about their order, and you said that we have removed three security organs from our units. Can you tell us briefly -- or, rather, can you tell us the Trial Chamber what was it that the Main Staff had ordered and why did you then remove the individuals in question?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about security organs who were removed from that position. Those cadres by and large came from the reserve contingent and they were not well trained, and that's why they did things that were not in compliance with the Law on Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission please. And let's look at the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having looked at this document, I'm not sure whether this is dealing with removal of certain individuals. Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said that three security organs were removed from their position or removed to another position. That's the interpretation I received. Since they were being removed -- actually, since they were being transferred, it means that they were basically removed. That's my understanding. Because they were unsuccessful in his duties. Perhaps if they were good at their job, they would have been promoted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: These three security organs have been dismissed, security and intelligence, and probably because of inappropriate attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, could you expand on that sentence, what it meant? As far as you remember, what does "three security organs" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking from memory, Mr. President, because I don't see a single letter of this document, so I cannot comment in any other way, save for what I recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you see the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can make it out now because it has been zoomed in. I do recall that some of the security organs were removed. But not only they, also brigade commanders were removed depending on their respective remits. It reads: "Up until now due to their unprofessional and irresponsible behaviour, three security organs have been removed (security intelligence organs at battalion level)." So the security organ at battalion level acted both as security officer and intelligence officer, so it was a double-hatted duty. What it says is what I've already said: They were removed due to their unprofessional and irresponsible conduct. They were not professional enough to go about that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question is whether you remember what kind of unprofessional and irresponsible behaviour this document referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those organs applied specific work methods that had to do with security and intelligence. They are trained specifically for that. The people who were appointed to these positions, well, the positions had to be filled although the people may have been insufficiently professional. However, they did not meet the threshold of professionalism and moral aptitude, since they did not have sufficient honesty, they did not value other people, they did not respect them, they perhaps acted inappropriately when dealing with captured persons - because they were the ones who processed captured persons, that may have been a problematic area, too - that was clearly identified and they were dismissed and other people appointed. I can tell you that we insisted on fair treatment concerning those who were captured. I recall a problem we had at Grbavica and two policemen were wounded there trying to protect some of the captured persons. So professionalism was required in their work when processing such persons as well as in terms of undertaking measures to gather and process intelligence. If they were not enough professional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. My next question is this. This document does not seem to refer to individuals forming the security organs. Rather, it refers to security organs that have been dismissed themselves. Could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not dismiss themselves. We say "organ," although it may refer to a person. So a security organ is a person. If that is the chief of the security and intelligence service, then he is the organ, rather than having the whole collective body which requires a system. But in this context, it pertains to a person, if this is helpful ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break or do you like to continue with your last document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have one last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 12362.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to address the term "they removed themselves." It's a reflexive verb in the English language and thus it may have been translated inappropriately or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, a moment ago you addressed the protection --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have gone through a mass of documents and we've got no notification of this one. This was not one of the almost 200 documents we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're referring to this one we are seeing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 12362. It was on the Prosecution's 65 ter list, but I just want to put on the record we've received no notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Yes, any explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, Mr. President. I'll look into it. But in the meantime, we apologise if it has, in fact, not been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that this is the last document, we can continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, item 5, please, you say that some people were injured by explosives or with a hand-grenade, a M75. And you say that the cause of the incident was the drunkenness of the soldier and his anger at not having been allowed to physically mistreat Muslim prisoners. A moment ago you said that you removed people for things like this. Can you tell the Chamber briefly what you did in such cases and whether the commands or commanders prevented individuals from mistreating captured Muslims.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly reply to that question. When I arrived, the initial prisoners arrived from Otes and they were Juka's fighters, some nine or ten of them had been taken prisoner, and they were treated fairly. Juka did his utmost to have them exchanged. We abided by the standards, stating that the captured soldiers and prisoners have to be kept safe. I recall an exchange which was supposed to take place concerning two captured persons. We had some problems at the brigade command to have them exchanged. They were known to have been criminals in the area of Sarajevo. Perhaps you recall that issue as well because Mr. Krajisnik came at the time to help me in dealing with the issue. So we always sought to exchange all those taken prisoner and we always strove to keep them save.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Perhaps we will have some additional questions after the cross.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, for the time being, this concludes my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break, as indicated, for half an hour. Let's have 35 -- we'll resume at quarter to 2.00. And we'll admit the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3487, Your Honours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin is on his feet. I thought I might give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did not want to interrupt my learned colleague, but I have a few comments to make about the transcript. For the sake of time, I suggest we do it now, but I could also do that later, as you please. It is your procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll have to find my notes, but it can be done very quickly. There are issues related to the French and the English transcripts. I would like to draw your attention to page 36, line 13. General Galic didn't say that it came from the corps but that it went to the corps. Page 37, lines 20, 21, two lines are missing about General Galic's answer. Page 10, line 23, for the French transcript, there was no reference to the Geneva Conventions but the Geneva Talks, "discussion de per Geneve" [phoen] in French. Page 10, line 21, General Galic never talked about people but he talked about assets, and I'm talking about the French transcript. I'm trying to give you the main points, Your Honour. There are other comments on former transcripts, yesterday's transcripts, but I have to review my notes about that. And, finally, I noted down that somewhere there is a declaration about Muslim air force, page 26, lines 21 and 22. And to be fully accurate, page 57, line 17, it's not: "Can you read" but it should be "I can read." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you did say about Muslim air force, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Galic wants to say something, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry, Your Honour, I was saying that I saw this on the transcript but maybe it was automatically corrected, and I'm talking about the English transcript. There was a mention about Muslim air force at the page that I indicated, but maybe it has been corrected in the meantime. So I just wanted to ask the Chamber to check if this is accurate or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in light of the -- some of the discrepancies or potential discrepancies, I would ask that the Chamber undertake an exercise where it order the language section to listen to the tape of yesterday's session as a test and compare it with the written English transcript and to make a track-changes version of the English transcript of yesterday, and then we will see from that what the extent of the differences are between what is being said and what is being transcribed. And based on that one day of testimony, we can decide -- or you can decide if there's any further steps that need to be taken to remedy the discrepancies between what's being said and what's being recorded in our record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we need it at the moment, but I'll hear from Mr. Galic first. Yes, Mr. Galic. Did you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to say that we did not mention Muslim -- the Muslim air force anywhere. We mentioned the Muslim armed forces. That was the extent of my assistance, in order to have a better formulation. As far as I remember, we did not mention any air force, but the armed forces. Thank you. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That sounds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry. General Galic, correct me if I'm wrong, I didn't think there was such a entity as a Muslim air force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not use such a term in my presentation. When asked by Mr. President as to what the MOS stood for, I replied by saying that it stood for the Muslim armed forces. If one were to use air forces, of course, it would be incorrect, because such forces did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Muslim air forces were -- were referred to when you were saying about the -- some Muslim people crossing the airport. So I take it that it should have read Muslim air forces, yes -- no, Muslim armed forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I agree, Mr. President. I agree with the last thing you said. I did not use the term "Muslim" -- the Muslim air force anywhere in my testimony. I agree with you that it is actually the Muslim armed forces. That is the correct term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the -- while the court reporter is transcribing the court proceedings at the courtroom, it is on a continual basis, on an ongoing basis it is reviewed on back door until it is produced as a corrected version. The Chamber doesn't see a need at the moment to take a step suggested by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I appreciate that. But I understand when it's reviewed it's review in English, so the tape is compared to what's been written to see if the court reporter has caught everything that was interpreted in English or said in English. So that doesn't really address the problem of whether what is being interpreted to us in English is accurate. It doesn't seem like a very big step to check by having somebody to listen to the B/C/S for one day. It would just take a few hours of someone's time. So that was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no need to change its position. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just one note for my friend Mr. Robinson. Of course Mr. Reid will be e-mailing our list of cross-examination documents immediately, but to expect additional documents related to the evidence today probably during the day and on Thursday sometime, given that I'm also involved with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more comment then. The Muslim air force has been already corrected as Muslim armed forces. And I don't think what we heard during the hearing was Muslim air force. What we heard was, rather, Muslim armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. But I think there's a dozen examples that Mr. Piletta-Zanin has raised over the course of General Galic's testimony where what's recorded in the transcript and what we heard is different than what was said. But I think our team will undertake this exercise, and if it's productive, we'll get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Galic, I'm going to be cross-examining you for the next few days, it looks like, but unlike Dr. Karadzic, I'm going to encourage you to answer my questions and answer them succinctly, and unlike your soldiers, I'm going to be interrupting you if I feel that we've gone off topic, and I just need to you know that before we begin. Is that all right? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's fine. We'll see when we start working if there are any problems. We are here to reach agreement to say what is important. What is important is to present the truth, and we have to arrive at it together.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now all these -- Dr. Karadzic over the course of your examination-in-chief discussed a lot of shelling and sniping incidents with you. And those were -- and you were convicted of all these incidents on the basis of having command and control over the units responsible for the shootings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question is -- the question is: You were convicted of all those incidents on the basis of command and control; is that correct or is it not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which incidents you mean, the ones I was accused of or the ones President Karadzic was accused of because there were incidents in my judgement that are not part of the indictment in the Karadzic case. That's why my question to you is: Are you trying to elicit a response to what refers to Mr. Karadzic or what refers to me, for which I was convicted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were convicted of every single shelling and sniping incident, scheduled shelling and sniping incident that Dr. Karadzic read out to you from his indictment; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were convicted on the basis of having command and control over the units responsible for those shootings of civilians; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to provide answers to such complicated questions. I really ask to be allowed to comment because it's very difficult to give a yes or a no answer, because I can answer but then we won't understand each other later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll get back to that later then and I'll help you understand. So where I'd like to begin from there is to go to the subject of protests and something that you said in your evidence in-chief to Dr. Karadzic. You said, as far as sniping incidents go, I do not remember a single protest that was lodged just because of a sniping incident. And that's at transcript page 37397. And in regard to shelling, you said, at page 37210: "As far as I remember," talking about the observers, UN observers, "As far as I remember, they never alerted me to the fact that the artillery forces of the SRK were acting in a way that would not have been legitimate." You said: "I didn't ever -- or receive ever information to that effect." So I want to talk a bit about that and ask you a couple of questions. You referred today in your evidence to Major Indjic. Major Indjic was part of the group for co-operation with UNPROFOR, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was the representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Main Staff for co-operation with UNPROFOR. Or the UN forces, which includes the UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he had his office in your command. That's where he was headquartered, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He had an office at the corps command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so it's correct, isn't it, that any communication from UNPROFOR went through him?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all -- all communication -- he was representative for the co-operation with UNPROFOR. Mostly all communication went through him but not all through -- not all talks went through him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Protests went through him --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protests went through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 4, it was not recorded that he was the representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Main Staff. The Main Staff was not recorded. This can affect the subsequent examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's the same type of issue. I do not remember if the French transcript is still interesting for anyone but me, but if it's the case, in Serb, General Galic said, page 78, that all written communications went through him, and I under lined the word "written," and you can't find this in the English transcript. I don't know if anyone is following the French transcript and can confirm this, but there are huge discrepancies because afterwards he might be asked or -- or be told, You said all communications, and General Galic will not understand that because he only talked about all written communications. So we should be very careful about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This time, Mr. Karadzic, you -- do you see a phonetic mark after Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and, although the -- court reporter missed this time, it will be reviewed and corrected in the course of review process. Rest assured, it will be corrected. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Bear with me. Yes, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we can get to the point this way. General, Major Indjic came to testify here and gave evidence in this case on behalf of Dr. Karadzic, and he explained how his office worked. Regarding protests he said - and that's at D2774 - it all went through the office of the liaison officers any communication from UNPROFOR, including protests. So it wasn't possible for such protests to be sent to someone in the corps command another way. It wasn't possible to bypass the office of the liaison officers. That's correct, isn't it? That's how Indjic's office operated?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, it's correct. Because I didn't speak English, so I couldn't communicate directly. Somebody had to translate it and Indjic was the only one who could do so. There were some other people at the command who spoke some English but not enough to be able to translate documents coming in or going out of the command. That's why this statement is correct. But I added before, if you remember, that at any other meetings with UN representatives, and I'm calling them that for you to understand fully, that he wasn't always present.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Major Indjic also told us, and it's at paragraph 85 of his written evidence, as I said before, D2774, he also told us that 95 per cent of the protests were in verbal form. That directly contradicts what you've just told us, or what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has said you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Indjic's interpretation, not mine. We must understand each other. He communicated orally with them. He received their protests and I received written protests, and I said here that I replied to each and every one. We discussed here to the extent possible. Oral protests could be stated in a conversation but they were not official protests. More generally speaking, all these protests -- there's a problem with all these protests, content-wise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's just stay on topic to talk about the system. Protests would come orally to the SRK because they were urgent; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oral protests were lodged with Indjic's office, I suppose. So it was his office, but for someone to call me up directly to -- to -- to launch an oral protest is something I don't remember at all. There were situations, if I may explain further, when there were meetings and talks about some problems, and then it was pointed out that this or that had happened, if you want to consider that an oral protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't? You don't consider that an oral protest?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just told us that: "...there were meetings and talks about some problems, and then it was pointed that this or that had happened, if you want to consider that an oral protest." Don't you consider it an oral protest, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's more of a warning and a discussion of problems, not a protest. A protest must have a certain form.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What form must a protest have for you to have taken action on it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own view of protests and what form they should have. If there's a protest about any sort of problem or incident, it should contain a basic textual part with all information about the incident in question. Then if a commission worked on it and dealt with the incident, there should be such information as well because without such information, if we're discussing at a general level, such as your forces fired at Brijesce Brdo, then three sides [as interpreted] should investigate, and in the situation that existed there was not much time to deal with such things. If I had received information of the kind that I think it should be, then I would have been duty-bound to take specific measures and measures to prevent any subsequent occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that if any protest that you might have received is not put to you writing, if it's not delegated to some kind of a commission, you took no action in regard to that protest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I put forward my view of this matter during the examination-in-chief. If I received information, and we've discussed such information protests here, I verified each such information with the subordinate commands to see what had been said or what had been written to me was, indeed, true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm doing my best to follow what General Galic is saying, and I think that I heard in the French transcript the opposite of what was said in the English transcript. It -- in French it says "c'est exact," it is correct, and in English it was the opposite. I do not want to break the rhythm and the pace of my colleague, but we should find a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Galic, did you say that it was correct or it was not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is difficult for me to answer your question. Whether what was correct or incorrect? So if you could repeat the question, then I would be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it to Ms. Edgerton. But before proceeding further, discussing this issue in vacuum does not help us much. I like to clarify what Mr. Galic meant when he said -- I will quote you're saying Mr. Galic. It's about protest. It's at the beginning of your answer: "There was situations, if I may explain further, when there were meetings and talks about some problems, and then it was pointed that this or that had happened, if you want to consider that an oral protest." What kind of problems did you mean, and what kind of conversation do you have in mind when you said pointing what had happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, we have seen from the documents shown here that there have been many instances of talks with UNPROFOR or UN representatives where many open issues were dealt with, not only incidents. It included matters such as supply, the passage of UNPROFOR, the exchange of prisoners of war, the passage of humanitarian convoys, and so on. There were other problems we dealt with and not only incidents. That's what I meant when I mentioned the talks. But when our attention was directed to an incident that happened, then I contacted subordinate units and had them check what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please. I believe it is important. Page 81, line 23, records General Galic as saying: "If somebody tells me in general that somebody shoots -- shot at Brijesce Brdo, then I must investigate three brigades," and it was recorded here "three sides."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you also recognise a phonetic mark there? Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is for Brijesce Brdo. But it should be "three brigades" rather than "three sides."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have your indulgence to find my path again, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, if I may, I would like to say that it is perfectly correct, because if I remember well, General Galic said, "for example," and it's recorded in none of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So maybe we can go back a little bit more towards the beginning, General, and you can confirm the following: Your corps received verbal protests; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your corps received written protests; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your evidence is that whenever - and I'll find your words to Judge Kwon - you said, in answer to a question from His Honour Judge Kwon, I think, or you said in your evidence: [As read] "If you received information, and we've discussed such information protests here, I verified each such information with subordinate commands to see what had been said or what had -- whether what had been said or what had been written to me was true." Correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mixing different things so it's hard to say with whether it is correct. But essentially it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You told Judge Kwon that in talks with UNPROFOR or UN representatives you discussed matters like supply, the passage of UNPROFOR, the passage of convoys, and so on. So, in addition to information about protests for shelling and sniping, issues were raised with you with respect to freedom of movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. To what extent?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's get back on track. General Galic, you said in your testimony in chief: "As for sniping incidents, I do not remember a single protest that was lodged just because of a sniping incident." And you said the same thing about shelling incidents. You were never alerted to the fact that artillery forces of the SRK were acting illegitimately. Are you saying now that you did receive protests about shelling and sniping and you acted upon them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have forgotten a very important detail here. I said during the examination-in-chief that there were individual sniping incidents and I never received protests about them. Neither verbal nor written. Nobody had ever told me that somebody was killed by individual sniping. There was some general protests. We said that during the examination-in-chief. I don't want the picture to be distorted. That's what I said. I adhere by that. There were general protests. As far as artillery fire is concerned, I said in the examination-in-chief that in documents there is no reference to artillery fire, only mortar shelling, and I said about every incident that was discussed here whether I was alerted to such an incident or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You spoke in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I refrain from standing up, but I have no technical means to find that part again, but I know that General Galic was very precise, and he said: "I'm going to explain to you the difference between artillery fire and other types of fire." And if questions are asked about artillery in general without making reference to what General Galic said, this is not fair. And then my learned colleague has the means to do that. She should quote the exact sentence. General Galic, when he talked about that, talked about artillery fire from a technical point of view, and he said that artillery was considered to be above a certain calibre, and I think that my colleague knows that, and that's why I stood up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, thank you for your intervention, but in this case we can continue. I think we can follow the context. Please carry on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you received protests about shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Protests about shellings themselves, there were such protests. We discussed those during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. You've now clarified these assertions in your examination-in-chief to -- to the effect that you didn't receive protests. Now, let's talk about these two types of protests. You said there were general protests and there were specific protests; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, correct. There were protests worded in general terms about sniping in a certain area. Or your artillery opened fire in a certain place. Or one or the other thing happened. Those were protests in very general terms, not backed by commission reports. And I said that it would have been good if all the protests had been backed up by reports, schematics, sketches, and only then would I have been able to undertake a -- specific measures. When it comes to mortar shelling, I told you, and you know exactly when I was informed, how I was informed, and in what specific terms was I informed about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why? What difference would a commission report have made to a protest that UNPROFOR laid across your desk? Why did you need a commission report to do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- do you have any protest in regard to any of the incidents in the indictment against Dr. Karadzic? Is there any such protest lodged with the command of my corps? I received a protest about the incident that happened on the 4th of February. I was not there. I received it through communication means, and I made checks based on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: What difference would a commission report have made to a protest?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- you know what? In the international law or, rather, when I used to deal with the international regulations, you know, it is defined what a protest is and what it needs to contain. It is defined in Protocol I what a report should contain. If -- it is supposed to contain a schematic for me to see, and based on that schematic I would know from which shell had come, either -- it would contain all the ballistic data, then I would be able to say: Okay, I have that information. This refers to that brigade and I'm sending a commission to investigate. Or if we were allowed, which we were not, to go to the spot to be part of a mixed commission and that commission had been set up. I gave you an example when we went to the airport to investigate and I told you what we established. Without that, madam, everything else is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that absent a commission report, protests to you from the United Nations were pure speculation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my answer, you could see that -- my answer to UNPROFOR that some of those protests were speculations. They were not accurate. And let me add also this: That if you receive a protest in this way, in -- worded in general terms, that you know based on some information from which directions fire could come and which units could have opened fire, that means that all that time we would have to investigate all the time. What would -- would we have been able to establish without documents? It would be difficult. At Markale there were a few commissions and what did they establish at the end of the day? At the end of the day, they established that nothing could be ascertained. That nothing could be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll get to Markale. But now --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was just a figure of speech, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just said in your answer that some of those protests were speculations and they were not accurate. Which ones, General, were not accurate? You should be able to give us some examples if you're making that assertion.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, to try and remember all of that after 20 years, all of the allegations, and to tell you, I have nothing in front of me. You have a book. I have nothing. However, can you try and remember when I answered UNPROFOR protests? I said that during the examination-in-chief it was said that we had opened fire on Colina Kapa, and I answered that at that time there were no Muslim forces at Colina Kapa. That was my answer. That was my reply. So I could have considered that speculation because after that there's my sentence, if you remember that, where I say that they didn't want to deceive us - I'm talking about UNPROFOR - they were just badly informed or they were not informed properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, you know, there was another general who testified in your case, General Abdel-Razek who was in a command position in UNPROFOR, and he came here during Dr. Karadzic's case. Now he said in P1258, his written evidence, that he took his complaints regarding the shelling directly to you. That's at page 15 of P1258. These points, he said, were the Serb shelling of UN headquarters and civilian centres. And I quote: [As read] "General Galic denied that the Serb shelled those areas. He said that the Bosnian side did the shelling. I recall that I told Galic, Listen, we're all military men. I tell you that we know where the shelling came from, it came from the Serb side. I have experience in these matters, and my staff and I have the means by which I can say where the shelling came from." Now, it seems like General Abdel-Razek coming from the United Nations, protesting to you about the shelling of, among other things, the UN headquarters, is not ill-informed at all, is he, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, I said something about General Razek. I said that he was not honest in our co-operation and that he misrepresented himself. You have to take with a grain of salt all of those allegations of his. I can't say what he claimed. I was not here so I don't know. I don't know whether what he said was accurate. However, a commission was sent to the airport to establish who had shelled the UNPROFOR command post and it was established that that was done by BiH Army, and the commission went out after his allegations. After that our commission was not allowed to attend any onsite investigation in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. If he had told --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before you go on further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the floor. I know what my role is here, and if I am to carry out my duty in full honesty, I should be able to check assertions made by the Prosecutor as it was the case with the Defence earlier on. I haven't received any copy of the documents used. Maybe it's a typo, maybe my colleague misspoke, but I should be able to check with a written document what the general exactly said, General Abdel-Razek. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure ... at the moment, it is left to the Defence to check the veracity of the previous witness's testimony as cited. And I -- I don't think you have access to the e-court. I'm -- why don't we continue at the moment. But I think witness has sufficient answers as to General Razek's credibility. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, yes, General, because you speak at speed, I interrupted you before we went on too far because I wanted to know about this commission you have just spoken about. And who was on that commission? I want the names of who was on the commission.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of all of the people. They were representatives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, our representatives, and that representative testified here at this Tribunal. There was also a representative of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army and a representative of the Sarajevo Sector. That was the commission that worked at that time. There was Lieutenant-Colonel Ugljesic on behalf of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't know about the other two side. He testified here. In the meantime, he has died, but you have his testimony on record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- so you're saying that General -- if that's his rank, Ugljesic is one of the people who was on this commission to deal with General Abdel-Razek's specific complaint of Serb shelling of UN headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. I shall speak slowly so nothing is omitted because it is very important. That was a mixed commission. Its name was a lower-ranking mixed military commission. On its composition there was a representative Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, a representative of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, a representative of the UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo. The representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, in that commission, was lieutenant-colonel - not general, we're not all generals -- or perhaps we are - but he was Lieutenant-Colonel Ugljesic. He testified here at this Tribunal. His testimony is on record. If you look at it, you will see that he testified that UNPROFOR forces were shelled at the airport and that the BiH army was responsible. And it was not the command of UNPROFOR that was shelled. It was the forces and assets of UNPROFOR that were shelled at the airport, not its command. And that's as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll leave that so I don't waste any more time. Now, you talked about the accuracy, if I can put it that way, of General Abdel-Razek about allegations that Serb forces had shelled the UN. And by the way, he said that they shelled civilian areas as well. I'm going to -- I wonder what you say about another individual who testified at your trial, and that was Major Bergeron. Now, Major Bergeron spoke about sniping, and at pages 11268 to 11270, he discussed his meetings with you on the issue of snipers. He said: [As read] "On several occasions where we would meet with General Galic or people or members of his organisation, we would often mention the fact that there were snipers and the fact that the snipers would kill civilians, be it women, children, and elderly people, for apparently no other reason than to terrorise the population than to demoralise the population." Is there anything inaccurate about Major Bergeron's evidence during your trial.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is all inaccurate. Everything is inaccurate. It was his arbitrary observation without any specific evidence. As far as opening fire on civilian targets is concerned, what do you consider a civilian area in Sarajevo? Were there any such areas in Sarajevo; civilian areas, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. The sentence: Do we have civilian areas is not on the record. Not "what do you consider civilian areas." [In English] Before -- before is "what do you consider a civilian area," there was a part of answer that is: "Do we have civilian areas in Sarajevo?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my question to your question. I was answering your question with a question, but I can answer it in answer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have that answer already, to a certain extent. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
