utterances.text: So what action -- pardon me. So because he didn't have any specific evidence, you took no action in response to Major Bergeron's assertions; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You spoke about his evidence here and what he said as a witness, as far as I can remember. And his allegations during evidence are controversial and contrary to what actually happened during the war. This is what I stated and what he said to me at the time. You know, when one comes here it's easy to talk about everything else, but did that major bring a document to show you and to tell you, This is what I handed over to General Galic. Maybe we could have then discussed that document to see whether he did hand it to me, to me personally, or somebody representing me. And now, based on his evidence on -- based on what he said that before the Trial Chamber, and you're inviting me to comment upon that, it's really difficult, and in my view it would not lead to a proper solution. As much as he can claim that something is true and accurate, to that same extent, I can claim that it is not correct and it is not accurate, unless he has proper evidence to corroborate his words.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What happens, General, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you because you seem to move away. Mr. Galic, your answer or, rather, your question was a bit confusing to me. What you did mean by asking whether do we have a civilian area in Sarajevo? Did you mean to say that there's no civilian area at all in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that part of the question was from the question that was put to me. The aim was to provide a more precise answer as to whether such areas were targeted. And as for civilian areas in Sarajevo, on both sides, and whether there were any such areas and what civilians areas there were, if any, I'm sure that we will come back to that later and that we will discuss that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your question sounded to me as if you were saying that every part of Sarajevo was militarised, so shelling any part of Sarajevo was legitimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's an erroneous opinion. I never said that. I never thought that. It never occurred to me to think that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And apologies. I'm having trouble keeping my stride this afternoon. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just based on your answer about Colonel Bergeron. I wanted to ask you, you said that - and I don't think you quite finished your sentence - that his evidence was not accurate and unless he had proper evidence to corroborate his words, and -- and you were referring to, I gather, his assertions regarding sniping. So I wanted to ask you, General, what happens when a military observer, one of the UNMOs, or somebody else from UNPROFOR calls your office and says, There's shelling in a given area and we know it's coming from your forces, what do you do? How do you respond? And how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anybody calling me directly, but they must have called Indjic and his Office for co-operation with UNPROFOR if anything like that happened. First, it had to be established where it was happening and what problems arose. I believe that then, if it had been established that the target was not legitimate, that fire ceased. That would have been justified. The duty officer was entitled to initiate that, not necessarily the commander, because the commander wasn't always at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of investigations were undertaken to establish where it was happening? Wasn't the word of UNPROFOR about where it was happening good enough for you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what would have been good enough to make a targeted investigation. We needed information about which side it came from, but there was no possibility of a commission investigating it. Then we had to know whether it was legitimate or not to shoot, whether there were forces there, whether there were civilians. I never entered that zone with my forces. I can show you where the forces were on that map. That was part of the deployment. And if you say that there was shelling from guns or mortars, anywhere in the zone, all I can do is trust you without evidence and then check with my subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Just before we go on too far, I don't think you've quite answered my question. Wasn't the word of UNPROFOR about where it happened good enough for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered what was required to make it good enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So unless UNPROFOR gave you specific information about which side it came from, unless you had a commission investigating it, unless you had information as to whether it was legitimate or whether there were civilians at that location, you didn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What kind of answer do you want from me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to know why the word and the protests of UNPROFOR, general protests - if you want to call them that - weren't good enough for you to take action.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I gave you an answer but I can repeat. We must put ourselves in a realistic situation. Every day there's combat activity. There is conflict. There's fire from both sides. In such a situation, you get a report about somebody firing at a certain zone. And then from the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, what kind of information would you be satisfied with to take measures in the corps? What kind of measures was I in a position to take then? I'll tell you: Unless I have the information that I mentioned, no commission, no this, no that, how do I find out from where, who, what? Because we're talking about 10.000 men. It's not easy to investigate who fired a shot at a window or who launched a mortar shell because that's the kind of information I need to launch a specific investigation. But, anyway, in the commands we would inquire over the phone, Did you open fire from this or that kind of weapon on this or that zone? And then we got either oral or written replies, because I can't know what's happening in Sarajevo if I'm in The Hague. It was the same then. Because I couldn't know everything that was happening at any given point in Sarajevo. We're talking about a large area with about 400.000 people, almost. Only in the area held by the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would like to be able to adjourn now because I also have a proofing with the next witness that needs to commence on time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I apologise. I didn't notice the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President just for, I think General Galic already knows this, but tomorrow we'll be hearing the evidence Mr. Yasushi Akashi, and he will not be brought back to the Tribunal, and we expect to have him brought back on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this may help, I would very much appreciate to get from the Prosecution a copy of the documents it is going to show, and anybody can make a mistake and that we have seen in the transcripts. So if I could receive a courtesy copy from Ms. Edgerton, I would be extremely grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without determining the issue, whether it's necessary or not, I'll leave it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honours, I would suggest that Mr. Piletta-Zanin contact Mr. Robinson, because Mr. Robinson has been notified of the documents. Because the length of time it would take to put together that collection of documents would adversely affect our preparation for the continued cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you, Ms. Edgerton. And I would recommend you to leave it to the Defence, as far as the correctness of citation is concerned. Given the time, shall we adjourn for today and discuss it further, if necessary, on Thursday? Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.03 p.m.,
